context.zh: 少時又無棋局，乃破荻為片，縱橫以為棋局，指點行勢，遂至名品。

translations.idiomatic: The emperor replied: "I have seen your twenty lines—among all my sons' compositions, yours is the finest.

context.zh: 但康樂放蕩，作體不辨有首尾，安仁、士衡深可宗尚，顏延之抑其次也。」

sourceWitness.quote: 晉征北將軍衞瓘以操為牙門將，數使於國，頗自結附。

context.zh: 衞操，字德元，代人也。

translations.literal: Wei Cao, styled Deyuan, was a man of Dai.
translations.idiomatic: Wei Cao, whose style was Deyuan, came from Dai.

context.zh: 少通俠，有才略。

translations.literal: In youth he mastered chivalry and possessed talent and stratagem.
translations.idiomatic: As a young man he lived by the code of the knight-errant and showed both talent and strategic mind.

context.zh: 晉征北將軍衞瓘以操為牙門將，數使於國，頗自結附。

translations.literal: Jin General Who Pacifies the North Wei Guan made Cao a gate officer; he was repeatedly sent to the state and rather attached himself on his own.
translations.idiomatic: Jin's General Who Pacifies the North, Wei Guan, appointed Cao gate officer and often sent him on missions to the Dai state, where Cao gradually built ties of his own.

context.zh: 始祖崩後，與從子雄及其宗室鄉親姬澹等十數人，同來歸國，說桓穆二帝招納晉人，於是晉人附者稍眾。

translations.literal: After the founding ancestor died, together with his nephew Xiong and more than ten clansmen and fellow-townsmen such as Ji Dan, he came in a body to return to the state, urging the Huan and Mu emperors to recruit Jin people; thereafter those of Jin who attached themselves grew somewhat numerous.
translations.idiomatic: When the founding ancestor passed away, Cao came home with his nephew Xiong and a dozen-odd kinsmen and neighbors, among them Ji Dan, and urged the Huan and Mu emperors to welcome Jin subjects. From then on Jin adherents grew steadily in number.

context.zh: 桓帝嘉之，以為輔相，任以國事。

translations.literal: Emperor Huan commended this and made him chief minister, entrusting him with state affairs.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Huan approved and named him chief minister, charging him with the affairs of the realm.

workerAuthoredIndependentlyHostApproved.before: Again, Records of Travel and Official Service carries the Yang Clan Genealogy, saying: The Yang clan of Tang's Xingxing lineage descended from the house of the Duke of Yue, originally from Zhongshan Xiangjie; the second son Ji begot Hui, Prefect of Luozhou; Hui begot En, Administrator of Hejian; En begot Jun, the Respectful Duke of Yue, who moved out to dwell in Fengyi; down to Zangqi, who moved to Xunyang.
workerAuthoredIndependentlyHostApproved.after: Again, Records of Travel and Official Service carries the Yang Clan Genealogy, saying: The Yang clan of Tang's Xiuxing lineage descended from the house of the Duke of Yue, originally from Jie, Chancellor of Zhongshan; the second son Ji begot Hui, Prefect of Luozhou; Hui begot En, Administrator of Hejian; En begot Jun, the Respectful Duke of Yue, who moved out to dwell in Fengyi; down to Zangqi, who moved to Xunyang.
workerAuthoredIndependentlyHostApproved.reason: 中山相結 is office 中山相 plus given name 結, not a toponym “Zhongshan Xiangjie”. 修行 is Xiuxing, not Xingxing.

workerAuthoredIndependentlyHostApproved.before: Records of Travel and Official Service also gives the Yang Clan Genealogy: the Xingxing Yangs descended from the house of the Duke of Yue in Zhongshan; through Ji, Hui of Luozhou, En of Hejian, and Jun the Respectful Duke of Yue, who settled in Fengyi, down to Zangqi, who moved to Xunyang.
workerAuthoredIndependentlyHostApproved.after: Records of Travel and Official Service also gives the Yang Clan Genealogy: the Xiuxing Yangs of Tang descended from the house of the Duke of Yue, originally from Jie, Chancellor of Zhongshan; his second son Ji begot Hui, Prefect of Luozhou; Hui begot En, Administrator of Hejian; En begot Jun, the Respectful Duke of Yue, who settled in Fengyi, down to Zangqi, who moved to Xunyang.
